title: Deep Dive II: The Clockwork That Cannot Stop
blurb: The host loop, springs and patterns. A program cannot stop early, so every loop must become a count, a tree, a table, or the same work on every item, and the four nouns become the four arms of a clockwork. One turn of the clock; springs squared into four numbers and fourteen operations; a ratchet that snaps at three hundred steps; two desks at ten and a hundred and twenty frames a second that match in every bit, in the repo's tests, because the frame you see is a rehearsal thrown away; tag 7 struck. Then the four shapes of a loop, each with its own machine, and two old names signed into the runtime, on screen. A finite machine paid off, an echo of Kleene and not a citation: the network is one fixed, exact step, and the host turns the crank.

shots.setting: a parchment plate · the host clockwork in silhouette behind it
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the thesis, heard slowly. CAMERA: locked on a parchment plate, then a slow pull back to the clockwork behind it. The chapter title inks in first (DEEP DIVE II · THE CLOCKWORK THAT CANNOT STOP) and stays. The quotation (Q015) is HEARD, not set: no sentence is inked on the plate. On 'program', under the title a STRAIGHT, ONE-WAY STRIP OF PAPER TRACK draws itself left to right across the plate, with a row of small stations along it; a small paper bead sets off at the left and crosses at an even pace, passing EVERY station, never skipping one. Along the track sit three tiny empty sockets, where a jump, a break and a repeat would sit, visibly vacant (no exit ramp, no points, no way back); one small label under them reads no jump · no break · no repeat. As the voice names the four nouns, four brass ARMS swing out from the hub of a HOST CLOCKWORK silhouetted behind the plate (escapement, ratchet wheel, a crank), each arm's tip a different small machine-shape (a peg rail for the count, a forked thread for the tree, a drawer for the table, a row of identical tiles for the same work on every item): shapes, not words. Just after the quotation (beat every), the bead reaches the end of the track and drops into the clockwork's tray; the escapement gives one tick and a NEW bead sets off from the left. The program runs once, straight through; the repetition belongs to the host.

shots.setting: the host clockwork beside the template's toggle switch · one frame
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: one turn of the clock, step by step. CAMERA: a medium shot on the HOST CLOCKWORK, set beside a small paper TOGGLE SWITCH (a rounded 52 × 32 px track with a thumb; a label gives its size). To the right, THE SOURCE TABLE from ch03-s04: a strip of 20 numbered pigeonholes (1280 and 800 in slots 0 and 1, event-flag holes, a four-card spring-matrix rack, state cards). Behind, the LOOM, small, in haze. On 'host', the clockwork's case lights: it sits OUTSIDE the loom, connected only by a crank. On 'toggle', a paper hand-cut cursor presses the toggle; a little PRESS in the clockwork stamps a paper TOKEN with the event and its time and drops it into a tray, and a bell-less paper flag pops up: frame requested (no caption: the voice says it). Nothing else moves yet: the handler has not run the program. Then the escapement ticks once per phrase of L0605, exactly in sync: on 'Inputs' the host slides the pointer and the event cards from the tray into their pigeonholes and four matrix cards into the spring rack; on 'loom' the crank turns ONE revolution and a wave of light crosses the loom's frames left to right, once; on 'copied' the next-state cards slide out of the loom's far end and back into their state pigeonholes; on 'page' the toggle's thumb slides along its track (the DOM moves from the outputs alone; a thin thread runs from the loom's output to the thumb). The step rail (one label) inks in along a rail under the clockwork on the first tick, and each tick lights its own phrase on it. On 'rests', between frames, the thumb has settled; the escapement locks and the clock goes silent; the requested-frame flag drops (no caption). Hold on the still mechanism.

shots.setting: a parchment plate · a brass spring stamp and a squaring press
shots.visual: THIS SHOT (one continuous shot, no cuts): springs without loops. CAMERA: a slow lateral track across a wide parchment plate, left to right, stamp then press then table; the equation is pinned to the plate's top margin and stays in frame. LEFT: a small paper window on a rail at 400 px, its destination marked at 700 px (a copper pin), the spring between them drawn as a paper coil; a 4 ms escapement on the host clockwork ticks evenly in the background. On 'multiplies', a 2×2 BRASS STAMP drops into frame with its four numbers engraved on its face as part of the object (0.9896 · 0.00328 / −2.6 · 0.82; HandwiredOS's stiffness 650, damping 45, one 4 ms step: SP02), and two input cards slide under it: −300 (distance from home) and 0 (speed). On 'moving', the stamp comes down with a dry clack; two cards come out, −296.88 and 780; the paper window creeps from 400 to 403.12 px and its coil begins to move; the one equation inks in at the top margin. On 'squared', the camera tracks right to the SQUARING PRESS: the stamp's plate is squared again and again, each fold a heavier clack, its exponent stamped on each folded plate (M², M⁴, M⁸ … M²⁵⁶), until one plate is marked M³⁰⁰. On 'JavaScript', a small paper LEDGER beside the clockwork (the host side) copies the four numbers off the M³⁰⁰ plate onto four cards, and the cards slide into four pigeonholes of the source table. Above the press, an OPERATION COUNTER with a step dial: as the dial spins 2 → 300 the counter stays FROZEN; on 'fourteen' the label inks in beside it. After the line (beat stiff), the ledger's stiffness and damping entries glow briefly on the JavaScript side, and a dotted line from them stops short of the loom (no caption: the picture carries it). Hold on the frozen counter while the dial keeps spinning.

shots.setting: inside the host clockwork · the 300-tooth ratchet
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the static bound. CAMERA: close on a large RATCHET WHEEL inside the clockwork, 300 fine teeth, with a release pawl; a pointer advances one tooth per 4 ms step. A long stall (a paper hourglass tipping) feeds steps in faster than the frame can take them; the pointer races round. On 'stops', at tooth 300 the RELEASE PAWL lifts: on the desk above (seen through the clockwork's open top), every paper window SNAPS onto its destination and stops dead, at rest; the backlog of unspent step tokens drops through a TRAPDOOR beneath the ratchet and is gone. A label: 300 steps = 1,200 ms. Then the ratchet resets to tooth 0, empty: nothing carries over (no quotation on screen). On 'every' (beat card), a TWO-SIDED CARD turns in the light, equally lit on both faces: one face drawn as a backlog of tokens carried on into the next frame (others carry the time), the other as the snapped, emptied ratchet (Handwired snaps); the single label names both faces. Neither face is struck: a design choice, not a mistake. Hold on the card turning slowly.

shots.setting: two paper desks side by side · one recorded session · 10 and 120 frames a second
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: two desks, one bit. CAMERA: wide on TWO PAPER DESKS side by side (split-screen held throughout), each a small HandwiredOS desk with one window, the same recorded drag replaying on both from a paper tape: the left desk flickers slowly, the right smoothly; each desk's brass plaque is cut with its rate, 10 and 120 (set dressing, not a caption). On 'familiar', a GHOST of the window on each desk follows the usual loop (handle the input, then step the animation by the frame's time) and the two ghosts begin to drift apart; the first label inks in and a DRIFT GAUGE between the desks swings, reaching 359 on 'pixels'. On 'saves', heavier COMMITTED CARDS (the kept state) are laid on each desk only at event marks and at evenly spaced checkpoint marks on the tape. On 'replay', each displayed frame is drawn on a sheet of CARBON PAPER worked out from the last committed card; on 'drawn' it lights; on 'thrown' it slides off into a CARBON-COPY TRAY and is gone, while only the committed cards stay on the desk. On 'tests', the ghosts fade and the two real windows lock into the same place at every shared timestamp; a BIT-STRIP (a row of 32 paper cells) under each desk shows identical bits, cell for cell, and the gauge falls to 0; the second label (the tests' conditions) replaces the first and stays to the end. No quotation on screen. Hold on the two locked desks.

Hold on the struck tag. TAG-LINE STAGING (meta staging.tagLine): ABOVE THE CLOCKWORK: the line runs high (40%) over the host clockwork, the camera low, looking up; tags hang above the turning ratchet; the pencil rests on the escapement bridge. LIFESPAN ENCODING (film-wide): a struck or ended thread drops to the rule at its measured lifespan; a still-held thread drops to its age as of 27 Oct 2026 and ends in a glowing open tip with a short copper arrow pointing right.

shots.setting: the prefix loom · the TREE arm of the clockwork
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a tree (running totals as a prefix network); the signature grommet paid. CAMERA: front-on at a small PREFIX LOOM: eight paper tabs across the top reading 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6; the totals row below them is the one equation. On 'row', a GHOST CHAIN first: one thread hops tab to tab, each join waiting for the last, seven knots stacked seven levels deep down the frame (a level ruler at the side counts 1…7). On 'pairs', the ghost chain fades and copper threads join neighbouring tabs in pairs, then (on the second 'pairs') pairs of pairs, then back down: the Brent-Kung pattern, four levels, each join a small knot of light; a ghost overlay beside it shows Sklansky's three levels, with one partial fanning into four threads at once; the level ruler now stops at 3 and 4. The totals ink in along the bottom row: 3 4 8 9 14 23 25 31. On 'three', as the level ruler stops at 3 and 4, the camera pushes in on two threads; then (beat sk) a PAPER NAME TAG lights in the film's tag style, SKLANSKY 1960, with the runtime's function name sklanskyPrefix in monospace, and under it a small caption, a prefix network only in a later reading (PT28); just after the line (beat bk) the second tag lights, BRENT · KUNG 1982, brentKungPrefix. Each tag carries a STAMPED brass grommet at its lower corner (the first stamped grommets in the film: the repo names these ideas in its own code). No figures are drawn for Sklansky, Brent or Kung. (Brent's own later note, Q164, moves to the sources page.) The two old names are NOT spoken: the tags, their grommets and the function names carry them in the hold.

shots.setting: the host clockwork turning the loom's crank · two chalk cards · a small repo card
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Kleene paid (planted ch02-s03); the deep dive's turn. CAMERA: a slow pull back to the whole mechanism: the HOST CLOCKWORK, its four arms folded home, turning the LOOM's crank ONE revolution per tick of the escapement; each turn sends one wave of light across the 130 frames and the next-state cards slide back into the source table. On 'finite', a faint echo of the ch02-s03 image appears in the haze above: the clock dial with a fixed ring of stops from Kleene's finite machine, and it settles over the loom, one stop per state (the ring is closed and countable: the machine really is finite). On 'outside', the camera finds the crank's HANDLE on the outside of the loom, on the host's side: everything unbounded comes from there. On 'circuit' (beat repo), as the narrator reads the lab guide's words, a SMALL REPO CARD in the docs' plain type hangs from the crank handle: the one text item, only the fragment a fixed-depth circuit with its attribution (Q127, the repo's own comparison, FR25). The crank keeps turning, tick after tick, through the whole hold. No other text. (Siegelmann & Sontag 1992 and Maass & Orponen 1998 move to the sources page as context the repo does not cite; if they are ever restored on screen, the Maass & Orponen card must read: contested: Siegelmann & Sontag (1994) claimed some robustness [FR15].)
